utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could the Registrar please call out the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-13a-T. Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic. For the Prosecution: Mr. Niemann, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi For the Defence: Mr. Fila, Mr. Petrovic

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me well? Thank you. We will now proceed with our next witness. May I ask you to -- yes, to stand and read out the formal declaration, the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fila, I may be wrong, but I think we have not received a statement of this witness, and I think it was given to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I can't find it in my file. It's probably because I'm a bit messy. All right. So I was wrong, so I apologise. Good. So you may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, did you make a statement to the investigator from my office on the 11th of May 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at it and see whether this is your statement? And I would like to tender it as evidence, Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 114 and 114A, for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is my statement and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections from the Prosecutor, I suggest that it be admitted into evidence as D114.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, did you graduate from the military academy of the Army of Yugoslavia in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you graduate from the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you graduate from the higher military political school of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you graduate from the school of journalism at the Yugoslavia Institute for Journalism?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you get your masters degree and what was your -- the subject of your masters degree?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990 I got my masters degree, and my subject was the main forms of implementation and the prospects of collective security of the organisation of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you receive a doctorate, and what was your subject?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I received a doctorate in 1995, and my subject was peacekeeping forces in the system of collective security with special reference to the characteristics and reaches of UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you the author of the book "Secession as Directed by the Great Powers"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you an active officer of the Army of Yugoslavia now with the rank of Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where are you employed now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I now work in the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the period that we are interested in, in 1991, rather 1990, 1991, were you an officer of the JNA, and what rank did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The rank of Colonel I received in 1989, so in 1990 and in 1991 I had the rank of Colonel and I was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What duties did you perform then in that period as a Colonel of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I worked in the Department for Public Information in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence -- in 1991, I mean. And immediately afterwards, when the peacekeeping forces came to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, I worked as assistant head of Department for Information for co-operation with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that is what we say, that you were the spokesman in 1990, 1991? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really, because according to the job descriptions we had then, there was no such person. I was just head of Department for Public Information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you issued press releases to the public and public information bulletins and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As head of the Department for Information in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and assistant head of the Department for Co-operation with UNPROFOR, participate in the working group that prepared a report on the activities of paramilitary units of Croatia towards the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of that group, and after that I helped elaborate this report and similar reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On that basis, could you please take a look at these documents. Is this one of the reports that was made by your department in this period? Please, I would like to have this admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit. Could you please take a look at the letter, which is there in the Serbian language, and is that the report that you have been speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is that report and the contents of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that report made on the basis of the information provided by the working group that you were in?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that is a report in whose elaboration you participated, and you say that it is your report, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did participate in its elaboration, and I fully agree with everything that is mentioned here

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I would like to have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a very extensive document, this is the first time we've seen it, so at this point in time we are not prepared to agree to admission into evidence. I apologise for not standing. Sorry. And, as well, I think that there are a number of issues in here which are addressed which we would have an objection to on the basis of relevance, particularly issues of cease-fire violations and blockades of barracks. If the court is prepared to hear this and does feel it is relevant, we will have extensive cross-examination on this and we have a substantial amount of materials that we would submit, both to this witness, and likely in rebuttal we would call witnesses on these issues. So if the court feels it's relevant, we are certainly willing to enter into that, but otherwise we would raise an objection to its materiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Two points. As for the admission into evidence, I mean, for the time being I think the Prosecutor has the right to go through this document, and so this item can be discussed later on, whether or not it can be admitted into evidence. As for the matters which are touched upon in this report, we also feel that the, say, breaches of cease-fire and other matters are not relevant to these particular cases. There may be matters addressed by Mr. Fila in his statement, but we feel now that they are no longer relevant, they are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest something in relation to what you said before we actually heard the witness and when we talked about the documents. Perhaps the Prosecutor will agree to this too. I have other documents as well, and we didn't even manage to have them translated. This one was translated only yesterday. So I suggest, if the Prosecutor agrees, that we see that all of this is there, and then once it is all translated, then in June the Prosecutor can say whether they agree that this be admitted into evidence. Perhaps they will agree to some things, they will not agree to other things, but there is no point in presenting arguments of this sort, you know, we are going to have a lot of rebuttal or this and that. I mean, this is frightening the other side, so I think we've had good co-operation and it's not necessary to present these kind of documents. So all of this, let it be recorded as Defence Exhibits. We are going to hear Mr. Williamson in June, and, if we agree on this, fine, and, if we do not, well, all will be well also. I haven't made any problems to you so far and I won't be making any problems now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would agree to Mr. Fila's proposal, if these are just all marked for identification and then we will have some period. Because certainly documents that we are receiving in Serbo-Croatian, it's going to be impossible to make any determination about them at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one more thing, sir. I'm sorry, may I just say one more thing. I received those documents only yesterday, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that we would all know what we are talking about, could you just give us a brief comment on the report, nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed? Thank you. As I said a few minutes ago, this report was made on the basis of documents, orders, decisions, reports of the then Federal Secretariat of National Defence of Yugoslavia. I had the opportunity of participating in this and I had insight into the written documents related to these events. This report relates to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it speaks of what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This report, first of all, highlights the most important points in this report, that is, there are the dates and days and even the actual timing, the actual hour, when the Croatian illegal formations or armed forces attacked the members of the Yugoslav People's Army, their facilities, property, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Briefly, is that the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that would do at this point. I mean, we have described what it's all about, so let us proceed. I kindly ask Your Honours now to submit only in the Serbian language, just for the purpose of identification, the documents which essentially prove how justified it is to present this first document. So please let them just be marked for identification and let the witness say what it is about, so that whatever this chamber does not agree to in June, I will certainly withdraw it. And that will certainly not be a reason for delaying the trial. I kindly ask the usher to show the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether meanwhile we could give a number to the other document which was received in Serbian and for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that would be document D115, the report. This would be D116. Yes, this would be D116.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at it and tell us what it's about, also briefly, like you did a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is information on the illegal import of armaments and military equipment from Hungary into the Republic of Croatia by agricultural aircraft of the Republic of Croatia in the period from the 20th of August until the 9th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the next document too. I ask the usher to kindly show the witness the next document. That can be marked as D117 for the purposes of identification.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is also information about the illegal import of armaments into the Republic of Croatia by an aeroplane of the Ugandan airline to Zagreb airport, and this information speaks of the quantities imported.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Colonel, at that time was the resolution on the embargo of importing arms into Yugoslavia in force?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This information was made on the 31st of August, however, the first resolution, 713, came out a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the next document now and tell us what it's about. What is this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is a numerical review of the representation of the nations and nationalities of then Yugoslavia in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that is the national structure, the ethnic structure of the Yugoslav People's Army's?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. First of all -- I mean, in the first column it shows the nationalities on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The next column shows population, the population of Yugoslavia, that is to say the actual number of inhabitants and also their percentage in terms of the total population. The third column shows the number of active officers, that is to say, officers and non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right, we have identified that. And what about the next page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the next page -- well, there is one more thing I wish to add. And that is that this document shows that this is the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, which was at that time a multi-national army. This is 1991. It consisted of representatives of all the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia. On page 2 is a list of Generals who were not of Serb or Montenegrin ethnic origin, and this was the situation of the 1st of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please mark this document for identification too? Please have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of a map this is and what it shows?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 119.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This map shows military facilities that the Croatian forces, the ZNG and the MOP (phoen) of Croatia on the 10th of November 1991 attacked, captured or assaulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the next document. Please explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D120.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the presidency of then Yugoslavia dated January 9th, 1991. This order was issued that on the territory of then Yugoslavia, SFRY, all armed units which are not under the armed forces of Yugoslavia or the Ministry of the Interior, so that such units should be disbanded, and also this equipment should be put into warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time was the presidency in its full composition, all representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by the president of the presidency of Yugoslavia, Milos Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what about this next document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D121.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a request made by the chief of general staff of the Armed Forces, General Blagoja Adzic, to the command of the fifth Army district, that is the Zagreb Army district, for the command to get into contact with the civilian authorities in Croatia. And, it says, that on the basis of this previous order that we had seen, to put under joint command 20.000 automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov type, and the rifles that were issued to the reserve forces of the police should be taken back, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, practically, this document relates to the implementation of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is orders to the commander concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this next document and say what it is and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D122.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please explain who signed it and what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by the Deputy Federal Secretary for National Defence, Admiral Stane Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he by nationality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: A Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From the 13th of August, 1991, he addresses the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Gregoric, and informs him that military equipment was looted, as it was being transported by railway on the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And who robbed this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This robbery was conducted by the members of the ZNG. They attacked the train, they disarmed the escorting officers, and they took 10 wagons full of military equipment, et cetera, which was being transported from the territory of Croatia to the FRY, or what is today at the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you take a look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document D123.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you briefly tell us what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the commander of the 5th military district, the Zagreb military district, General Zivota Avramovic who informs the general staff of the armed forces of Yugoslavia about the fact that -- he is informing him about a great massive grouping of the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Croatia around certain facilities in certain municipalities where there is a majority Serb population, to concentrate the forces of internal affairs and it states which directions, in which areas they should be grouped. For example, in Kostajnica, 400 members have arrived, 600 elsewhere and this document is dated the 4th of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what period does it encompass?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This document of the 4th of July encompasses a period -- characteristic of the provocative attacks on members of the JNA from the 27th of June to the 30th of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now take a look at the following document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document D124.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might intervene just a moment. Might I suggest that the gentleman could identify all of these documents in globo as documents that he is presenting and then we can just wait and have the translations and determine if they are relevant. It's impossible for us to cross-examine on these because they are in another language that, unfortunately, neither of us can read. So all we have to go on is what he is saying. If he can just identify them and then we get the documents in English, we can make a -- I think an informed decision as to whether we would admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Judging from the brief description given so far by the witness of the various documents which have been presented by the Defence counsel, we feel that most of these documents, probably all of them, are irrelevant to our case. We are only interested in those documents which directly touch upon the situation in Vukovar. So therefore I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's inside. Your Honour, if I may. In all those reports include Vukovar, but they haven't been translated. There is mention of Vukovar. They are for the whole territory of Croatia, which includes Vukovar. So Vukovar is included in the documents. And when the documents were drawn up, we did not know that there would be hearings of this kind so as to focus on Vukovar itself. But they do include Vukovar. This is the last document that I have in my hand. This is the last document to be marked for identification, and I have two more which have not been translated. So it will be easy for us to see in June what is relevant and what is not relevant. There is no problem there, once the documents have been translated. As I say, this is the last document. Otherwise, as I say, all the documents refer to Vukovar. They include Vukovar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But, of course, Mr. Fila, when I mentioned Vukovar, I meant to say that they explicitly, express mention should be made of Vukovar in those documents. If they generally describe the whole situation in the Republic of Croatia or touch upon matters such as, say, breaches of cease-fire or prohibited importation of arms by the authorities in Zagreb, these are matters which are not relevant to our particular case. We are dealing with a very specific case, and the issue is whether or not the accused is guilty or innocent. Innocent or guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I did not bring Wheeler to testify here, so I must respond, if it is not relevant, then, very well. Then nothing is relevant. Wheeler isn't relevant either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Fila, I said before, I mentioned Wheeler on purpose, to say that, of course we were at the outset of our proceedings, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. I have given you the last document and that completes the document bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something else. It is document D125.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This document deals with a request for all the police departments. That the members of the reservists be taken to the reservist, internal affairs department, and it is signed by Deputy Internal Affairs Minister Dzelko (phoen) Tomanovic. That is the document I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The defence has completed its set of documents to be marked for identification now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I now would like to ask you something else. As a relevant question, the question was raised of the uniform of the JNA in the Vukovar period, particularly the pilot's uniform of the JNA. And two witnesses, if you recall, identified these. Now, I have a small technical problem in this regard. The original documents are in colour and we are dealing with colour, are we not? So I can just hand them over to you and if you have the technical possibilities to photocopy them, please do so, because I do not. Whereas the instructions as to how these uniforms are worn, I have this in five copies, but once again, unfortunately, only in Serbian. So once again I request that this be translated later on. And this is Defence -- these are Defence exhibits. Would the usher come and collect these documents, please. That is the technical part. Yes, it is not possible to -- you have it in colour. The witness would have to see these in colour, so could you give him an identification, mark it with an identification, and then hand it to the witness. First, the second piece of evidence is what we want. The second is just the law on how the uniforms are worn. The second document is actually what the uniforms look like.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D126.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There are two different documents. So we need two numbers for identification. Mr. Garmes. There are two different documents as I say, two different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you first -- have you received the first document, the one over there. First have a look at the black and white document that we are going to show you. Have a look at D127 first, please. The photograph and what it is about. First have a look at the photographs, 126. Could you tell us what they depict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I suggest that these be displayed on the ELMO, since we don't have copies ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot about the ELMO. They are going to put it on the ELMO for you on the right-hand side, and then everybody will be able to see. Mr. Pavlovic, the usher will do it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at the uniforms, please, now, on the ELMO, and speak into the microphone. It's a bit difficult, but try please. These are the official, daily uniforms of active military personnel at the ground forces, the winter uniform and the summer uniform. Which is the summer, which is the winter?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The winter uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please show us with your finger or pointer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is the winter uniform, suit and cap, trousers, shirt and cap, and the daily uniform of the parachute units, the winter ones with the overcoat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Would you take a look at the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This shows the official daily uniform of active military personnel of the aviation and the anti-Air Force defence, the winter one with the overcoat. The official daily uniform of the aviation and Air Force defence, winter, once again with a coat, and the daily uniform of active military personnel of the Air Force, the summer uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we have a look at the next slide, please. Would you describe that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This shows the rank and insignia which are worn if an active officer -- active officers worn in front on the left-hand side on the breast when a raincoat is worn, an overcoat is worn, and so on and so forth. These are the different ranks, the Major, Colonel, Lieutenant-Colonel, and these are the Generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we see what an Air Force Colonel wears.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: And the Lieutenant here, so two wide ones -- one wider one and two narrow ones and three narrow ones and one wide one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the material used?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It is metal. It is made of metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at the next slide please? We have no more slides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila I would like to see these now, please, the originals. Can we see the originals here. I want to see them now while they are still in mind. Would the witness please look at this exhibit. And I am now looking at -- I don't know the number of it, but the exhibit in which the person shown is in the greyish uniform. Would you look at that and tell us if that's the colour it appears as you look at it. Is it a good representation of the colour or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: You are thinking about this one here? It is the official daily uniform of active personnel of the ground forces, yes, that's -- that is the colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The ground forces, is that the army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The ground forces, the army, yes. It is of a greyish/green, olive green colour, greyish, olive green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that is a good representation, is it, in your judgement? Does it look like that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's not clear enough, but that is the colour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you a Colonel of the ground forces? Do you wear that uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colour is the uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As I say, greyish, olive greenish in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it more green or does it move towards the green colour more or is it more grey in colour?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Predominantly greyish or greenish. Greyish, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if we can have an exhibit number for that so that we can avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, might we also have an opportunity to look at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When we complete everything and then I'll supply you with a set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would rather have a number now, because otherwise we are going to get confused. Can we have the next number and mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number D126 and it is document 126A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I could just get some clarification. Which is 126 and which is 126A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got this exhibit as 126.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think that's 127, what Judge May has in his hand. Judge May is holding 127, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This one is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is D127. The black and white documents are D127. The black and white documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the army then, the army uniform, the colour one which we have on the ELMO, that is 126; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The colour document is 126, the one we actually showed is 126A whereas the other documents are B, C and D.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the next document, please, which shows the Air Force uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, if you wouldn't mind. There are some matters I want dealt with next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are ranks as well, and I wanted to complete this and then discuss matters. There are in colour, the ranks in colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter that we want to deal with while it's in our mind. Would the witness look at this exhibit which we've been shown, which I think is the Air Force uniform. Very well, 126L. Is that the Air Force uniform, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The first picture here, this first picture, has been crossed out, but don't let that trouble you. It is not actually topical now, but it was the uniform worn at the time. It is a 1989 rules governing uniforms and clothing. So it is the official daily uniform of active officers of the Navy and descent units with the overcoat. The next is the official daily uniform of active officers of the Air Force and anti-aircraft attack with the winter uniform with the overcoat. That is the second picture. The following one is the official daily uniform of active officers of the Air Force and anti-aircraft defence, winter with the overcoat, and also the daily uniform of active officers, Air Force, the summer uniform without the overcoat. And that is -- those are the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the figures shown, as we look at them on the right, are the Air Force uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just to -- that there is no misunderstanding, how many of these uniforms are Air Force?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: All three are Air Force, but this one here is with an overcoat, the second is with a coat and the third is only the trousers, the jacket and the cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do the higher officers, the Lieutenants and First Lieutenants, did they all wear uniforms of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And your rank too, the Lieutenants and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the uniforms we wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you just describe the colour, the last one on the right, the Air Force, without the coat. What colours are those? The trousers, the jacket, and then the shirt and the tie, what colours are those?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The colour of the uniform is sky blue. Air Force and Air Defence, sky blue colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the shirt?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The shirt is blue, light blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the tie?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Dark blue or navy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I also ask you a question. Are there any sort of casual jackets worn by members of the Air Force, because I -- normally army personnel tends to also wear some sort of jacket which are more -- less elegant and formal than the overcoats we see here in the two central figures. I wonder whether there is any -- any such sort of jacket, particularly in winter, for winter jackets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are no other clothing -- there is no other clothing, apart from the ones shown here. These are copies from the rules and regulations governing the clothing of the Air Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In practice members of the Air Force never wear some sort of different jacket -- they only are obliged and in practice they do wear either the jacket which we see here on the right-hand side, or the overcoat, which we see in these central figures?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a pattern from the pilots. They have pilots' jackets, which are characteristic, once again, for pilots. But this is -- the regulation clothing, regulation uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What is the colour of the pilots' jackets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Similar to these colours here, blue, but they are characteristic intended to change in practice. They were not always the same. They had fur, or without fur lining. They had sleeves, tight sleeves around the wrist, or not so tight. They were different. They tend to change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Belts on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please tell us now, in war what were all the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army wearing, the pilots and the others, the Air Force and the others?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Under conditions of mobilisation war, all the officers wore camouflage uniforms, that is the coloured, multi-coloured uniforms, which are uniform for all the branches of the army, of the Yugoslav Army of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can we say that in November 1991 all the officers of the JNA who were active around Vukovar had to wear the -- I'm sorry -- the camouflage uniforms, olive green, of the multi-coloured type or the ones you showed us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a rule everybody was to have worn camouflage uniforms, the mixed colours one, with a beret, and they wore this in 1991, in the war operations around Vukovar, yes. Regardless of what branch of the army they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And these are the official uniforms when they go home, when they go to the general staff, these are the daily, regular uniforms that are worn, so to say, in peace time from their homes to their place of work and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us clear this up. Of these four uniforms that you have before you, the first on the left is the Navy uniform; is that right? What colour is that? What colour is the Navy uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It is the same colour of the olive greeny greyish colour as the ground forces, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that the period that is relevant for us, 1991, November is the month, that the JNA had daily uniforms of the type you have shown us, the Air Force as well, and under war conditions that prevailed in 1991, around Vukovar and further afield, but we are dealing with Vukovar, that regardless of the branch of the army they had to wear camouflage uniforms. Very well, yes. Now, would you like to explain to us what insignias they had. And look at the other documents that you have before you. May we continue, if you agree, with the insignia? Would you explain them to us, one by one. They are also in colour. What is this in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are ranks, ranks of officers, ranks of officers, made of metal. I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. But please could we mark this and -- camouflage uniforms did people wear these ranks made of metal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These ranks, the insignia, were put on only if a raincoat was worn -- a raincoat, and if one wears a war uniform, this kind of insignia are placed on war uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is a war uniform like, you said a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's a camouflage uniform, the multi-coloured one, how should I put this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So if a Lieutenant-Colonel of the JNA in November 1991 was in war uniform, what did he have to wear?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He had to have this insignia here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of his breast.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Near his heart?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, near his heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he have something on his shoulders, on his epaulettes ?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, if he wore this in front, then he didn't have anything on his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Has this been marked? For identification I mean. All right. So could we please continue. What is that? Black and white?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you give a number to the -- this last -- yes, to the insignia document, I mean the picture of the various insignias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the paper that you have on the ELMO, rather than the paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is uniform of active officers with the rank of Colonel and General of the Air Force and the Air Defence for winter and summer, and this is a ceremonious (sic) uniform, for example, there is one for holidays, for the day of the JNA, particularly for that -- those acts of service, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So could we please mark this as 126, whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: What is this that we are showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 126B.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are you showing us now, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is one on epaulettes, these are insignia worn on epaulettes, on the uniform. These are the lower ranks, soldier, Corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this is document 126 again and now the next one, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are non-commissioned officers. This is a Corporal, yet another Corporal, then a Sergeant, a Staff Sergeant and a warrant officer, first class and second class.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So those are non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are insignia of ranks of Army, Air Force and Air Defence, so that is to say Corporal, Sergeant, warrant officer; second class, warrant officer; first class. And at the same time these are the insignia used for students attending military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document we are looking at now is 126E.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are insignia worn by officers Lieutenants, First Lieutenants, Captains, Captains; first class, Major. There is a district difference here. There are two stripes here, as you can see, so Lieutenant-Colonel, Colonel. These are the insignia that were worn then and are still worn today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please explain something to me now. What about Lieutenant-Colonels and Colonels, how do you compare them to the others?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is the rank shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How do you wear it on your shoulder?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This way along the shoulder, see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Not this way, not crossing the shoulder?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And are the stars always one next to the other or is there a star and then empty and then another star?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, this is -- this is the way it is done, so there is a star that is closer to the head and the one right next to it, I mean for example the two stars cannot be at this end. It can only be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And they can never be put cross-wise?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm afraid we have not received copies of these documents. Did you only hand in one copy in colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Only one. I asked for your permission, Your Honour, to have the registry copy this in colour for you, because we haven't got colour photocopying machine. Next please. Oh, yes, could I ask you something else.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 127F.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last subject on this. Look at the Colonel's insignia. Can a Lieutenant-Colonel wear this by pulling out the middle star, or do the stars have to be one next to another?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They have to be placed this way, and it is not placed by the person himself. That's the kind of uniform one buys with these insignias. So this was already done at the workshop where these uniforms were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this and tell us what you are showing.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are Generals, Generals, Major-General, Lieutenant-General, Army General, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this that you are showing now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are Admirals' insignia in the Navy, so it is Admiral, Vice Admiral, Admiral of the Fleet, and here is a Corporal and the highest rank is Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this also -- is this also worn along the shoulder blade, like the others?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, along the shoulder, yes, like the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 126H. That is the document that we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are we looking at now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are ranks that are worn on the sleeve in the Navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. You don't have to go into all the details.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Corporals -- Corporal of the Frigate all the way up to Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are insignia of Admirals, all the way up to Admiral of the Fleet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please let us see what this is, 126G: And finally, what is this at the end?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is also the official daily uniform of active army officers, winter uniform with an overcoat and another coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what colour is this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Olive green, grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say SMB, what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying olive, green, grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And we have completed this particular line of questioning. And I ask for this to be admitted into evidence. This is 126K.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now, Your Honour, I wish to show 127, Exhibit 127. These are rules and regulations, again unfortunately this has not been translated either. We've just received it. This is rule on military uniforms of the armed forces of the SFRY. From when and how long was it in force?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This rule on the uniform of armed forces -- of the SFRY would be in force from the 1st of January 1989. All these photographs that we have seen just now belong to these rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And do you have something special on Air Force officers there, Colonels or Lieutenant-Colonels from the Air Force? Is there something specifically related to that and if there is, you could read it out. If not, then we shall move onto further?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No -- do you have something that is worn in war, wearing a war uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, read that to us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: "The war uniform is worn by officers" -- slower please. "War uniform is worn by military men in the following situations at mobilisation and during a state of alert, extraordinary circumstances, mobilisation and war."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be all. Colonel, the last question that I am interested in, could you tell us how the Army districts were organised during the time of the SFRY? Was this according to republics or was it not according to republics, or was it according to some other criteria?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time there were Army districts, in terms of organisation. There were five of them. The Air Force and Air Defence and the Navy, that is a total of seven. The commands of the Army districts were in the capitals of the republics, respectively. Their territory did not coincide with the territory of a specific republic. It is well-known in all armies that operation, strategic lines are organised according to the assessments of the top state and political and military leadership, so one Army district could include the territory of one and part of a second and a third republic even, if necessary. If that is what you are referring to, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I had in mind. No further questions for the defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions on unrelated issues, but the bulk of my questions would be on these uniform points. And we were unaware that this witness would be testifying about this. There was nothing contained in his statement. So I would request a recess of approximately 30 minutes, if that would be possible, in order to prepare this. We have some material that we would like to present to the witness and it is going to take us some bit of time to get it together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about the famous pictures --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have those. I will bring those when I return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Fila has -- yes, he has an engagement until 11.30, I think. So I suggest that we take a 40 minute --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I always seem to be interrupting you. Sorry, I'm not really that impolite, but I have just received a piece of information saying that the meeting has been cancelled. So I don't have any engagements. I just heard about it a second ago. I'm sorry for interrupting you once again. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Don't worry. All right. Thirty-minute recess? Is it fine? So we will resume -- reconvene at 20 past 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, before you start, let me again restate that we intend, and as I said before to Mr. Fila, we intend to disregard many of the points made by Dr. Wheeler in his testimony, those points which are not relevant to our case. Therefore, I wonder whether you could refrain from tackling issues which we regard as immaterial to our case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. My questions on the issues of the documents that were submitted are very limited, at most five or six questions, and then I'll move on to the other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: First of all, Colonel, I want to clarify something. Right before we went into the break, you indicated that in 1991, there were five military districts as well as a Naval district; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Air Force was also counted, the Air Force and Air Defence in the rank of a military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there were five districts in total, including the Naval district and the Air Force district, or were there five Army districts and then an additional Navy district --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, seven, a total of seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, in fact, weren't there only three Army districts? The fifth Army district situated at Zagreb, the first Army district situated at Belgrade, and the third Army district situated at Skopje, and then a Naval district situated at Split?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The Naval was in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you were incorrect then when you said that there were five military districts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: There was the first district, the second, the third, the fifth, and the seventh, which makes it five, plus the Navy district and the Air Force and Air Defence district.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where was the second district situated and the seventh?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember at that particular time where it was, but the fifth was the Zagreb district -- the first, Belgrade; the second, Nis; the third, Skopje; the fifth, Zagreb, and the seventh Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show you a military district map from 1991, and can you tell me if this is incorrect, and I will mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit, I believe it will be 207; is that correct? Two hundred and seven.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, P207.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Because isn't it a fact, Colonel, that the district lines were redrawn in 1988 and that, in fact, Ljubljana and Slovenia came under the fifth military district at that time situated in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The lines were redrawn, and some military districts were conjoined, but I can't tell you the details of that redrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So do you have any reason to disbelieve this map that I have displayed to you which shows three military districts situated respectively in Zagreb, Belgrade, and Skopje. And then perhaps, if this might assist you, I will show you an exhibit which I will mark as 208, which shows the various Army corps within those districts, and it indicates there was an Army corps situated in Ljubljana and an Army corps situated in Nis but that these were both within other military districts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, have you got any further copies for the Defence and for the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not, Your Honour. This is something again that was put together in quite a hurry in this break, and we were rushed as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have nothing against the Defence showing all this, but could you explain why this is more important from what I submitted earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my response to this is Mr. Fila asked this question at the end, and this gentleman -- he asked where the military districts were and how they were set up. He raised this issue. We didn't object. We should have the right to cross-examine on it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This gentleman has presented himself as an expert on the JNA. If he doesn't know where the military districts are within his own Army, I think that is indicative of his expertise in this field. I think this is a legitimate area for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you one thing. I cannot, at this point in time, tell you that in 1991 what military district encompassed what borders, what towns, because very often what happened was that there were changes in redrawing military districts into Army areas, Army districts, but I can say with full responsibility that this was never -- we never took detailed account of the fact that one republic should have exclusively in its area its own military district. Those kind of borders were determined according to the strategical and operative or operative strategic needs and assessments of the supreme state and military leadership. That is why, at this point in time, I really can't tell you what towns, if they were on the borders, between the borders of two republics or in parts of a republic, to which military unit -- district they belonged to. In concrete terms, the command of the third military district encompassed my own native town of Vranje, which is in Serbia, and it goes up to the town of Leskovac. So we are talking about operative strategic lines and directions. Of course, that is no longer the case. But it did change, lines were really redrawn, and I apologise for not being able to give you a detailed overview of all this at this particular time. If you need information of this kind, we can get detailed information for each year, and that is no problem. We can supply the court with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a couple more points on this, Colonel. I'm not asking you where each village in Yugoslavia was located in terms of military districts. I'm asking you the total number of districts and where those were headquartered, and so I understand that you are not in a position to say, if towns that were on borders, where they were located. But I think that this is a pretty simple question as to how many military districts were there in the JNA in 1991, because, in fact, there were no redrawing of lines after 1988, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a detailed answer to that, a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, would you agree, Colonel, that in autumn 1991 that the JNA and forces of the Republic of Croatia were engaged in armed combat?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the whole of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the autumn of 1991. Would you tell me if, in the autumn of 1991, the JNA and the forces of the Republic of Croatia were engaged in armed combat?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to allow the witness to answer fully before interrupting. Let me repeat that at the beginning of 1991 and only around mid-1991, in the second half of 1991, the first, so to speak, armed combat began, not between the JNA and the Croatian Armed Forces but it is the Croatia Armed Forces, the paramilitary forces, illegal forces, attacked members of the Yugoslav People's Army, the military facilities, the army barracks, army property and so on and so forth. Therefore, it is a question of the attacks launched by the Croatian paramilitary formations on the Yugoslav People's Army. The members of the Yugoslav People's Army, according to its character and according to the constitution, were duty-bound to defend the constitutional order of the state, the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the country, and that was still Yugoslavia. It was a unified country, the unified country of Yugoslavia, and the JNA fulfilled that task. First of all, in separating the conflicting parties, between the Serbs and the Croats at that time; and later on, when the barracks were attacked, when the barracks were blocked, it had to defend itself and the lives of its members and army property.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Colonel, you have not answered my question. My question was to you: In autumn of 1991, was the JNA and forces of the Republic of Croatia engaged in armed combat? It's very simple. It's a "Yes" or "No" question. If you need to explain it further, please do, but can you answer that question? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Armed combat was waged in the sense of defence of the military facilities, the barracks, and the members of the Yugoslav Army who were being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me, are military installations legitimate military targets during a time of war? Again, "Yes" or "No," and then explain as you need to. It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about a civil war here, an armed insurrection, not a war in the classical sense of the word. Therefore, military installations which are located on Croatian territory and the barracks there were there for 50-odd years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Again, I will ask the question: Are military installations legitimate military targets during a time of war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, theoretically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, these figures that you have presented to the court for the composition of the JNA in 1991, in fact that was on the 1st of January, 1991, was it not, which is marked as Exhibit 118?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And those figures changed significantly during the course of the year 1991, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Those figures changed somewhat, to a certain extent but, in actual fact, the Yugoslav People's Army, right up until the end and at the beginning of 1992, remained of multi-national composition because it continued to have offices and generals and junior officers from all the nations and representatives of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: By April 1992, Serbs and Montenegrins made up 90 percent of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That piece of information is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is not? By April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not. 1992, you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection. April 1992, is it relevant? Is it a relevant date to what we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my next question I think will make it relevant, but he has answered it, and so it's not necessary to ask the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will ask you then, if you would look at this document very briefly, which we'll mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 208. I do have copies of this. And as this is being passed out, if you can tell me, would it be a fair assessment to say that Serbs and Montenegrins were over-represented in the officer corps beyond their share of the population?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, allow me to explain, please. The Yugoslav People's Army was truly of multi-national composition, and I can tell you that strict attention was paid to having all nations and nationalities represented in the Yugoslav People's Army, especially when it was a case of senior officers and generals. And the fact that, for example, there were less Slovenes in comparison to the number of inhabitants, I can tell you that the Slovenes came forward less frequently for service in the army than Montenegrins, for example. The reason for this I see lies in the fact that Slovenia was an economically well-developed republic, so young men rather chose to enter into business rather than the army. On the other hand, there is a tradition in Serbia and Montenegro that the Serbs and the Montenegrins had greater affiliation for the army, they liked to serve the army. So that whenever a competition for military schools and academies came up, they were open, they were publicly announced in the media, radio, press, television, and depending upon the number of applicants, the personnel were selected for the military schools and academies. I can tell you that as a regular practice, there were far less applications from Slovenia and partially from Croatia as well, and there were far more applicants from the other republics. That was the reason why, as the army had to be fulfilled with a certain number of officers, this was one of the reasons that the state of affairs was as it was, which I do not consider to be of such importance because, in actual fact, the Army, as I say, was of multi-national composition as long as it existed as the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My final question on this point then is: You indicate that there were 28 non-Serb Generals at the beginning of 1992; I believe the date on that was January 1st, 1992. Can you tell me what happened to the other 30 or so Generals in the meantime between April of 1991 and January of 1992, the other 30 Generals of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: A certain number of them left the Yugoslav People's Army, and in view of the present political situation and situation in general, they joined up with their republican armies, so that they themselves, by their own free will, left the Yugoslav People's Army. Those who were of retirement age were retired, not only those of other nationalities, but this was the case of the Serbs and Montenegrins. I'm talking about the Generals here, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would offer this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 208 -- I'm sorry, is that 209?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 209.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object, not because we don't think this should be adopted, but then I think you should adopt as a Defence Exhibit a list of the Generals of national composition of Yugoslavia for 1991, 1992, to which Prosecutor Williamson is against, and now he is using this by the same token -- to tender this. So it is a question of principle. I don't mind, I have nothing against that, but, if you are against the list of Generals as being accepted in evidence, why do you want your exhibit to be accepted? If we accept both, then I have no objection because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we should reach agreement on this. I'm sorry. I agree with what Mr. Fila's saying. That's fine. We will be happy to delay submission of this until after the other exhibits have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. All right. So it's P209 only for identification purposes, not yet admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you indicated a few moments ago when you were testifying that there were very strict rules for uniform wear within the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the JNA is concerned, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And these rules were scrupulously observed during the conflict in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the members of the Yugoslav People's Army, yes, the rules were scrupulously observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this time, I would like for you to be shown a video clip which comes from Prosecutor's Exhibit -- it is the video compilation, I'm not sure of the exact number of the exhibit -- but it is in the booth. I believe it is ready to go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's fine. We see a variety of uniforms there. Now, certainly Major Sljivancanin, who is talking to the Red Cross representative, is wearing a camouflage uniform. The other people around him, some of them are wearing regular solid green or SNB overcoats, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The camouflage uniform was compulsory uniforms for all officers in the JNA at the time, NCOs; whereas the others, I don't know about them. They were probably various improvisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like for you to view a video which has been marked as Defence Exhibit 2, if you would, please? We will start the portion where everyone arrives at VELEPROMET. What I would like for you to do, Colonel, is to identify all the various uniforms that we see in this photograph and to which army groups they belong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This uniform there. The first man that went by in camouflage, this dark camouflage colour. Right there.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is not a uniform of the members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If it can proceed, please? This man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That too is not a uniform of the JNA. They are improvisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the man at the gate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This uniform here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is a uniform without insignia, without a cap. I don't think that it is a member of the JNA. I wouldn't say that it was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This uniform, these uniforms here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is not a uniform worn by a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Neither is that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, this uniform, would it have been possible to purchase something like this at a shop in Novi Sad, say, some kind of army surplus store?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible. It was possible to buy some uniforms, and there was the possibility of exchanging on the spot, on the spot, to exchange uniforms and combine uniforms. So that some of those who were not members of the JNA, such as the ones you can see here, wore different uniforms and were in the locality, on the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you: What happens to someone when they leave the JNA, if they retire from the JNA? What happens to their uniform? Do they keep it? An officer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The uniforms, when an officer retires, the remaining uniforms he has, he is duty-bound to return. But there were cases when the uniforms were not returned. They keep the uniforms but don't have the right to wear them after their retirement. And most of them like to keep their uniforms as a souvenir of their army days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's understandable, I assume. And there were a lot of instances of guys showing up wearing uniforms from World War II or from the 1950s or 1960s, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But those were people who, at various ceremonial occasions and other various events, were invited to attend and then to invoke their memories concerning certain events in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While we were watching this videotape, we saw this photograph of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know him but I -- from the information media, I was able to see that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, he was heading up a paramilitary group in the Vukovar area. Can you tell me what the relationship was between the JNA and these paramilitary groups that were fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. First of all, it is not correct that Arkan was in the paramilitary units, and that is incorrect. It has not been ascertained as correct and it is not. If the Prosecutor is interested, he fought within the compositions of the JNA, but it is not up to me to say, it is up to the Prosecution to prove that he was at the head of a paramilitary unit. That is not correct. If that is relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is relevant. It is indeed relevant. So I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the relationship was between the JNA and Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I was not on the battle front, I did not take part, and the involvement of the units on the spot is something that is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you have written a paper about Croatian paramilitary forces. What is your understanding of paramilitary forces on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that paramilitary forces existed. I know that there were volunteers who volunteered to offer assistance to the Serb population who had begun en masse to go to Serbia as refugees. Now, the relationship between the Yugoslav People's Army and those volunteers, I really don't know, and I cannot tell you about that relationship. And let me repeat: I was not on the battle ground, I did not take part, and therefore I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you familiar with General Andrija Bijorcevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In fact, he was commander of the Novi Sad corps, and from the 4th of November, 1991, he was the commander of Operational Group North, was he not, which was operating in the Vukovar military theatre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which units took part and who their commanders were, nor am I familiar with their behaviour on the ground, and I'm not familiar with the activities that were carried out in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, these volunteers from the Serb side that you were talking about, were these under the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, you've done this extensive study on Croatian paramilitaries. It seems like you would have some idea of what was going on in your own army.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: But, you see, I was interested, first of all, in the situation and attacks on members of the JNA because Croatia had seceded, went through violent secession, and that was the backdrop against which I wrote a book about this later. So I was personally interested in following this, and I also had certain data officially. And we informed the public about this; we wrote press releases and prepared reports for the competent authorities, for the federal government, the Federal Ministry for National Defence, et cetera, that was my duty, and the rest I'm really not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you did not think it was relevant to this study to know what was going on on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The basic thesis of my study was to prove that violent secession was carried out, that this is a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, it sounds like you had pre-formed opinions as to who was to blame if you weren't willing to look at both sides of the issue; wouldn't that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was only in 1996 that I wrote my book, and I was only interested in this facet. Someone else could prepare the other facet, write about it, analyse it, but I really couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like for you to view a videotape, if you would, please, which comes -- it was originally shown from Beli Manastir television, January of 1992, General Bijorcevic talking about his relationship with paramilitary groups in the Vukovar theatre in 1991. And I will mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 210 and the transcript as 210A, which includes both one in Serbian and one in English. If you would, would you tell me if what General Bijorcevic is talking about is consistent with the policy of the JNA? If this can be run now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This can be forwarded to the part where General Bijorcevic is speaking. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the policy of the JNA: to surround a village, to send in volunteers, and to kill those who refuse to surrender?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, by no means.
