However, the formation of the Serbian region of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem these incorporated villages that had only heard about me and had not known me personally and the people were fairly nationalistically coloured and considered, and they do so today, that I betrayed Serbian interests. And Mr. Hadzic, in his first attempt to place me in the government, proved unsuccessful, and when he tried on the second occasion at the people in Beli Manastir to take the rostrum to convince people that I should be a member of the government, in view of the fact that there was -- there were not enough professional men. And I think that is the main reason why they elected me to the government, because I was a professional man. The majority of educated people lived in the towns and as the towns were outside the control of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and the cadres from Vukovar were expelled from the Croatian and Serb nationality there were not people who could perform this job professionally and I think that is what spoke in my favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, the nationalists didn't like you much, of either nationality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Both the Croats criticised me for being a great Serb and the Serbs accused me of being at the service of the Croats and working in their interests, and I'll probably suffer here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that government was? Did you receive a salary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an unsuccessful attempt to organise something in this situation of disarray. The government had been functioning for several months and viewed on paper and administratively something might have been -- you might have said that there was a kind of organisation. But in actual fact it was a time when war raged and where the basic instruments of implementing power and authority was something that the government did not have. So it was not able to establish its authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have a salary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have a deputy assistant, a cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I had one and a half offices in the Ministry for Agricultural, which was located in Erdut with three assistants and one lady, she was the administrator. I had two graduated agronomists and two doctors of science. If necessary, I can give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's not necessary, thank you. Can you tell us of your relationships with the army and Territorial Defence, the whole government and you yourself, you personally. What were your relations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the area -- in the area of the villages, each village, there was a defence of the village organised with its command and its commander. In the majority of cases we were dealing with people who had -- I don't want to be too strict in saying this -- but they had extremist views and imposed themselves through those extremist views. I was lucky because the commander of my village was not like that and so I was less -- it's not the right expression, but I was not mistreated. I had a little more freedom, perhaps, to put it that way. And practically all the power in the villages was in the hands of the headquarters of the village defence. That was at the beginning. Later on, with the arrival of the army and a decision of the assembly, all this was placed under the control or tried to place it under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army for the greatest part this was implemented. So that the government, neither before nor afterwards, had any practical parent authority. Some agreement could have been reached, perhaps, but the government had no authority over Territorial Defence, particularly not the Ministry of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any police and army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tanks, planes, anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when you moved along the territory, could you tell us what territory are we talking about that your government tried to control?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The territory was part of the Vinkovci Municipality, the Vukovar Municipality, a portion of the Municipality of Osijek and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they compact, were they conjoined in one whole?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I was never in -- in most of the places, I never went to most of the places. It was very difficult to reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have to have a permit by the army to be able to move around?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you controlled? Were there checkpoints when you passed through?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: At each village, and this is a later period, that is to say September, somewhere at the end of September in each village there was the Yugoslav People's Army, which was stationed there, and at the entrance and exit to the village there were control points set up so that the control was regular and you were not able to leave the village without a special permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The fact that you were a member of the government, did that help? Could you say, "I'm a member of the government, I am the Minister of Agriculture," that seems to be very important for the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army did not recognise our government, including the soldiers who considered themselves to be stronger than the Minister of Agriculture. So very often I had a lot of problems, precisely for the fact that I was Minister of Agriculture and because it said on my permit that I was Minister of Agriculture and they sort of laughed at me, it was a laughing matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you couldn't order an officer or the whole Yugoslav People's Army, you couldn't issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. With some officers, lower ranking officers, one could establish contact. I already said that I did things related to agriculture, and since this entire area was full of the army, it was -- it required quite a bit of effort to organise some kind of production, primarily harvesting, the autumn harvest. So with some lower ranking officers one could establish contact and people could be allowed to get to certain plots of land or to move along certain roads in order to do the agricultural work that was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have trouble with them asking you to give -- you to give them people for the army and you needed them for agricultural work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. To work in agriculture was humiliating and it -- it at that time was very fashionable to be a soldier, and this was considered to be a small thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think until January 1992. Well, four or five months, I think, yes. Four or five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And which government came after you did?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: After the Republic of Srpska Krajina was established, which elected its own authorities, the assembly and the assembly chose a prime minister designate. I think it was Mr. Zeotrinic (phoen) and he chose his own ministers. I was not in that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that was your ministerial career, those four or five months?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why were you not elected to this other government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. You were a still an agronomist. They still needed a Minister of Agriculture. What kind of people were elected then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I probably didn't suit them because I had trouble with Knin afterwards too, so -- I imagine that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What's the reason? Your positions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of positions, political?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, political.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think that at this point in time, Your Honour, it would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we'll take a 20 minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, we stopped at the point when you were no longer a member of the government of the Serb autonomous district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. A government was set up, as we heard, in the republic of Srpska Krajina. You were not in it, so what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 1st of June, I didn't do anything. I was at home. On the 1st of June, I was appointed director of the Vinarija in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please tell us the year?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remained in that position until 1994 when I was elected President of the Municipal Assembly again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a good point to show you a document and to ask you what this is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D133?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document signed by one of my associates while I was Minister of Agriculture. This was signed by Mr. Vidovic. This is a certificate showing that I worked at the Vinarija and he became director of the Vinarija after I did, and this is a certificate saying that I was director of the Vinarija from the 1st of June, 1992, until the 1st of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So could this please be admitted into evidence, D133, and the translation will be D133. Before we move on to your new election as mayor, please have a look at this next document. What does it show? This is Defence Exhibit D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D134.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does this document show?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your passport. It was issued where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what does it say? What citizenship did you have at that point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Croatian citizenship, and I had Croatian and Yugoslavian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did all Yugoslavs at that time have republican and federal citizenship?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you had a republican citizenship of the Republic of Croatia and federal citizenship of the state of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please show the serial number of your passport and from where can one see that it was issued in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The passports were such that the first letter shows the Republic and mine was H for Hrvatska, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could this please be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please now look at this next document. Would you explain what we can see from this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D135.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document that you have in your hands now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of my refugee ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is refugee ID mean? Could you explain this situation a bit? What is a refugee ID? Why did you get it and who got it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: My family got it when we moved to Sombor in 1996, my wife and I, because I was on the list of Serbs who did not receive an amnesty from the Republic of Croatia, and with the establishment of this authority on that territory now, which was, until then, under the control of the UNTAES, there was a danger of my being arrested and that's why I left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can I say that now you have the status of refugee in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you cannot. I am a prisoner and My Lady, wife, is a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the last valid citizenship you had was the citizenship we saw on this last passport, and that was of Croatia and of the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And practically now you do not have citizenship and your permanent residence is at the detention unit in The Hague; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I am going to show you this next document. Could this previous document be admitted into evidence, if there are no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D136.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document that you have in your hands?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a military ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does it say in your military ID? What are you? Who are you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: My military service in Krusevac in Yugoslavia in 1975. I went there as a regular soldier, a conscript, and then I left as a Private. I was actually in charge of a particular company, but only in terms of administrative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And could you look at this now. Participation in war. Can you see that rubric there? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does that prove?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, to summarise, you did your military service in the JNA as a Private?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And during this war, in relation to which we are having this debate here, you did not have any functions as an active or reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not mobilised at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, on the 20th of November, were you a Lieutenant-Colonel of the Yugoslav Air Force?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. That is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you take at that look at the next document so that we could ascertain your military status? Could you explain to us what this document is? Could the previous document be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D136 (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What can one see from this document, Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate issued by a military post called 3001 which certifies that as they check through their military records, professional military men of the JNA, the Slavko Dokmanovic from Vukovar was never an officer or a non-commissioned officer or a civilian person serving in the JNA or in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And please, could you take a look at the last paragraph? No, no, no, sorry. I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit. I made a mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are we speaking of D137?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There's a mistake in the transcript. The registrar said document D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could we please have the next document shown to ... And with this, we would end the military career of Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic as far as Defence Exhibits are concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D138.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate of military post 3065 from Novi Sad from the area covered by the Novi Sad corps and that is the area in which I lived, that I was not a member of the reserve army corps in that area in 1991, 1992, I was not in their records as a reserved officer, reserved non-commissioned officer or a soldier in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no objections, I suggest that this be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now let us continue. In 1994, you become President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar once again. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the elections that were held in 1993, the Radical Party won. I was an independent candidate and I won the election, but due to certain problems -- and I don't want to go into all of that now -- the Deputies were not satisfied with the work of the President who belonged to the Radical Party, that is Mr. Vukicevic, and they asked me, the coalition of the socialists and the SDS, because they could not agree on who they would choose as President, probably, or for some other reason, I can't know that now, they suggested that I be the new President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar as an independent candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you were not involved in any political parties, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you think? What is the reason why you were elected?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say what my opinion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you about your opinion.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The city was destroyed and a little bit was done in terms of restoration, but practically nothing was happening. Instead of getting more and more inhabitants, we were losing inhabitants. People were unsatisfied with the work of the assembly and the assembly organs. More could have been done, and it is probably for that reason that they proposed me as President. I appointed Mr. Teofilovic, the Prime Minister designate, and he proposed a very successful local government, and over a very short span of time, they built quite a bit in Vukovar -- not to enumerate all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, do enumerate it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We repaired almost 70 kilometres of road. Most of the waterworks started operating once again. We made seven electric power plants or stations. A marketplace was built so that the people could get proper supplies, three schools were repaired. A bus station was built. We fully repaired 25 apartments and 150 were supposed to be completed during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, could we say that you were elected as a man of peace because the times of war were slowly going by?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was never in favour of the war. People knew that. And that was probably the case. People there had had enough of the war, at least reasonable people had had enough of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And someone needs war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your career, I mean, during this last term of office of yours before you were replaced, could I ask you why you were replaced? When?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: After Croatian operations vis-à-vis the Republic of Srpska Krajina, only a part of our district remained peaceful. There were quite a few advocates of war. I must say that we did not use a single bullet, we did not fire a single bullet while all of that was happening there and one really had to invest one's authority in order to do that. It is difficult to speak from this position now and it was even more difficult for me to speak in that position then, and we entered negotiations, and these negotiations ended with quite a few problems, but they did come to an end with the signing of the Erdut agreement. And I was one of the participants in the negotiations because of the extremism of the people who were against signing any kind of agreement with Croatia and who were in favour of continuing war, pressure was being brought to bear against me again, and that led to my replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, could you please take a look at the next document? What is this? Who is inviting you and what for?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D139.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an invitation to a seminar in Liechtenstein that was addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why was it addressed to you? What were you then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now take a look at this document? Could this document please be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have an objection to this. It's just getting a little bit off the issue at hand here and being irrelevant, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you speaking of D139?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should explain this immediately. We are not getting off the issue because these are documents which show the personality of the accused, and this is my duty, and that is what we agreed upon at the beginning of this -- these two weeks. So I'm talking about his reputation as a mayor and what he was like as a man. That's all. After all, you have to know what kind of person we are talking about. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this next document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We do admit D139 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at the next document I have just given you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D140.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is information through Mr. Milanovic, who was head of the negotiating team during the negotiations. This is from Mr. Bell on behalf of UNTAES. It was sent to me, that I would be visited by a delegation of the Council of Europe on the 10th of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could this document please be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D141.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections or, rather, perhaps you could explain first what it is and then ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an interview I gave to Dnevnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what do you speak of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I speak of peace and the restoration of normal life in the area. We are trying to explain the Erdut agreement to the people to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could this document please be admitted into evidence as Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Next Defence Exhibit would be an entire set of photographs. Mr. Dokmanovic is going to explain each and every photograph, and they should be marked as D142 A, B, C, D, et cetera. Everyone has five copies, as needed. Immediately after this, I am going to fulfil Mr. Williamson's wish and I am going to move on to concrete questions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first photograph is from the Zagreb airport where we are shaking hands with people who were in charge of our security while we were there for negotiations. This man was shaking hands, Mr. Milanovic, Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Bell. I can't remember the date exactly, but I think it's November or October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So these were negotiations that were already underway?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: These were negotiations that we were supposed to have in the Assembly of the United States of America in Zagreb, but due to certain problems this did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a photograph which was taken. I wish to say that Mr. Modalek was also in our delegation. He is the first one you can see here. He is a Croat by nationality. Mr. Lakic, Mr. Loncar, Dokmanovic, Milanovic, Hadzic, Mr. Galbraith at the same time. This picture was taken in the Embassy of the United States of America in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Next one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is from a meeting that we had in Erdut with the Croatian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In relation to the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the signing of the Erdut agreement. These negotiations were held by Mr. Galbraith and Mr. Stoltenberg. There were other people from the European Community, but the two of them bore the brunt of these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Next?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is also a photograph of a meeting -- probably the result was successful because we're all smiling, Mr. Galbraith, Mr. Milanovic and Mr. Hadzic and myself. This is in Erdut where I am shaking hands with Mr. Galbraith. We have the interpreter, the UNTAES representative, and Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are you doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I am shaking hands with Mr. Galbraith. I don't quite say what we're handing over here, but it is from the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes? Would you explain that picture?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an artwork which, as President of the Municipal Assembly, I was presenting Mr. Galbraith with, and on the back it says "Peace comes with those who bring it."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you were replaced, therefore. Can this be adopted as D142, whatever? And then you were replaced as mayor, you left for Sombor, and we'll leave the other events.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain this. I was replaced in an unusual way. The assembly meeting was called without me, and they wanted to discuss the Erdut agreement again, to re-examine it. I gave my word that we would recognise and implement the Erdut agreement, not only myself but stronger people than me, both politically speaking and in every other way, and the agreement was adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. After that, as I said, a list was published of 250, I think, if I'm not wrong, a number of 250 non-amnestied (sic) Serbs from the region, and I left for Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was this? When did you move to Sombor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In June or July of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: About one month after the indictment was brought against you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My children chose to remain in our family house for one year. I visited them from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Certain individuals have appeared here as witnesses, and I'd like to take you back now to the reason for our gathering here, and that is November 1991. The headquarters of your government was in Erdut, and you saw a tape, you listened to the witnesses, and I'm going to ask you where you know certain individuals from. Where do you know Jova Cvetkovic and since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known him since 1990 as President of the Municipal Assembly of Jagodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you friends later on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we became close and friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the same case with Nebojsa Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known Nebojsa Lazarevic from the conference of towns of the Danubian countries held in Belgrade in the Intercontinental Hotel in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of the individuals who were important, how do you know Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known Goran Hadzic from earlier on, our villages are in close proximity to each other, and while I worked in Vupik, I was his immediate chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know the individual Arkan, and since when and how?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We said hello from time to time, sometimes not. He was stationed in Erdut, and I saw him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have to pass through his barricade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The road to the government, led by the camp, and that was where an obstacle was set up, a checkpoint where they stopped us regularly and asked for our IDs. Sometimes they recognised some individuals, not everybody had to show their IDs, perhaps some people didn't, but in any case there was a barricade set up, a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that was the only relationship that you had with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I never sat at the same table with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the indictment raised against you, you have three more names, Mrksic, Veselin Sljivancanin, and Radic, Captain Radic. Do you know those individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic I saw from a distance of 20 metres, on one occasion, I think that it was in 1995. We never became acquainted. Captain Radic, I don't know him at all. And Veselin Sljivancanin, I got to know him in the Vukovar Days held there, where we presented the economy of Vukovar, and our artists, musicians and poets, had a programme there. I don't know who invited him, but we met there on the occasion. We did not talk more than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1994, 1995. I was President of the Municipal Assembly. I can't quite recall. It was not -- whether it was in 1994 or 1995. But the host was the President of the Municipal Assembly of Podgorica and he invited guests to attend. We attended that meeting as guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After you had spent some time in Sombor, you came into contact with the organs of the prosecuting office in The Hague. How and when?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic called me up, I think it was at the beginning of 1997, and he had also left Vukovar and was located in a village, was staying in a village near Belgrade. He asked me whether I would agree to speak to the representatives of The Hague Tribunal. I said I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in his house. I think it was February 1997. I'm not quite sure. It was winter at any rate. Mr. Purkovic and I went in our own car, we went there and we talked to a lady, I don't recall her name. Boro Savic and Mr. Milanovic were present on the occasion. Later on, on several occasions, we talked by telephone, I don't know who I talked to, but at all events we had several telephone conversations, and I was once asked to come to Vukovar. I said that I could not because there were the Croatian authorities there and they would probably arrest me as soon as they saw me. And so we decided to meet in Sombor on the 24th, I think it was, of June, last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you talk about during that meeting? What did they ask you? Well, not on that day. In general. In general.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we discussed what happened in Vukovar. The subject, according to what I was told and in my interests, not only because of me, but for others, to clarify what had happened in Vukovar in 1990 and 1991. So the subject we discussed was Vukovar, and, as far as I remember, in those two days of talks, we did not arrive at the date of the 20th of November. I think we left with the 2nd of May and tried to throw more light on the events of the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I take your mind back to those key days of the 19th, 20th, and 21st of November, 1991? Would you cast your mind back to those particular dates? Would you tell me where you were on the 19th of November in the morning and carry on from there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th, in the morning, I was in Erdut. There was a government meeting in the morning which lasted for about one to one and a half hours. After that, I went to Backa Palanka. I returned from Backa Palanka to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you meet Jova Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the late afternoon hours I met Cvetkovic, and I think that was how it was. I would remember, had I known that I would be brought to trial, but in general Mr. Cvetkovic, Mr. Lazarevic and myself met that evening. Mr. Leskovac was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you went to your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you spent the night in Trpinja in your own home. Who were your guests?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Cvetkovic, Lazarevic, and Lazarevic's driver, I think his surname was Ivezic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there a lot of people staying the night in your house, as they said, that they slept on the floor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The times that are now behind us, but which were ahead of us, meant that there was a lot of coming and going in my house. People came daily from Vukovar and they had -- wanted somewhere to spend the night. My house has not -- is not completed, not all the rooms have been furnished to accommodate overnight stayers, so people had to sleep on mattresses on the floor. I don't really remember. This is not something that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this brings us to the 20th of November in the morning. Would you carry on from there. As far as you recall, what happened on the morning of the 20th of November, when you got up? What did you find?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th, I woke up, I got up about seven, half past seven. I think that was the time, more or less. I can't tell you the exact minute. My wife had already -- was already up, Cvetkovic was already up, Lazarevic and Ivezic had already left. I must clarify this, if I may? Lazarevic came a day earlier, and he said that a delegation from Kladovo would be coming with humanitarian aid on the following day, and that he had agreed that they would come to Backa Palanka -- that he would go to Backa Palanka, that he would have talks, I don't know exactly, but that he was to have a meeting with them in Backa Palanka. As that was the agreement -- why it happened like that, I don't know, but we decided, Jova Cvetkovic and myself, to go to Backa Palanka ourselves and, according to the conclusion of the government, we were to be in Vukovar on the 20th. So we went to Backa Palanka. I think Cvetkovic, myself and Ivezic came at about nine, half past nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So on the 19th you had a government meeting in Erdut; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were the minutes kept?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You saw the minutes when we brought out the witnesses. Are those the same minutes? Do you need to have a look at them, or can you identify them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to ask me questions from the minutes, then let me have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you show the witness D53, please, Exhibit D53? Would the usher show the witness Exhibit D53? Defence Exhibit D53.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember having taken part at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present, quite certainly, quite definitely, but I don't remember all the details. So I'd like to read through, please, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you take a look at item 5, and do you remember what it is about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That the government of the Serbian district be above the JNA units on its territory, superior to the JNA units on its territory. We had a lot of problems. I think that everybody had a lot of problems with the army. We had some ambitions, that is up to the Defence Ministry, not the Ministry of Agriculture, and from that side, that is where the initiative came from, I suppose, that the army be placed under the control of these civilian authorities; namely, our government over the army was nil. Our contacts, at least my own contacts and most of the contacts of most members of the government, perhaps some members of the government had more contacts, but officially there were no relationships between us and the JNA and the armed formations and the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you able to place your government above the units of the JNA ever?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. Perhaps I will be wrong in saying, but Mr. Stipe Mesic took the stand here when he was president of the presidency of the SFRY, and he clearly stated who was able to command the JNA and how can a replaced President of the Municipal Assembly command the army if the presidency of Yugoslavia was not able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, item 3. Could you explain to us the sense of the meeting held on Wednesday, the 20th of November, in Vukovar, the last paragraph, below the item we discussed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That a meeting be held on the 20th of November, 1991, in Vukovar. According to the information we had, the operations in Vukovar, military operations in Vukovar, had ended, and the President, when he proposed this, had the intention of having the members of the government appear in Vukovar; and in that way, to show people that civilian authority existed, at least on paper, if not in reality. In my view, it was an attempt, in the town in which we were not at all popular and we had absolutely no control, not even in harmonising views and discussing matters, that this should appear on that day so that the people, or what was left of the people, could see us there, could see our presence. The meeting was not compulsory, was not mandatory -- I forgot to say that a moment ago -- so that -- and I think that was what was said, that it was not mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So because of that and because of Nebojsa Lazarevic, you decided more because of Lazarevic than because of the meeting itself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response) I think it is the right time to show D2, the tape marked Exhibit D2, as of 10.00, when he comes -- and his arrival in Backa Palanka. Every time that you see yourself appearing on the screen, would you say so and would you say when you hear your voice, say it is your voice that you are hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is not Dokmanovic. Play the tape further.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you recognised yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you show us, please? Tell us when --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Continue with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying something there at that point.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we speed up the tape a little? All right. Now. Where are we now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the Orthodox church in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which means that you're going from Backa Palanka to Vukovar. So that destroyed house is in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what we saw a moment ago was. This is the Vinarija. We are at the entrance there now. That's the entrance to VELEPROMET. That was our rallying place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was to meet there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the people there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were people who had left the basements and cellars and had gathered there. I don't know who gathered them. Probably the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznjatovic. That's me. Mr. Vasic and Mr. Kosic. Myself, Kosic's voice there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we now move the tape to 3.00 p.m.? Mr. Dokmanovic, at what time was that government meeting held, the meeting we mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was about 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: About an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know who took part in the meeting? Who can you remember having taken part in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prime Minister, Mr. Hadzic; the Vice Premier, Dr. Hadzic; Miro Micenogorac (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They are Ministers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some other people that I did not know. There were some Assistant Ministers. I can't quite remember. There was such a crowd at the VELEPROMET compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a military man there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting? There was an officer at the meeting. I don't know whether he was a Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel. I think that he took us into the room. I did not enter first, so I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you discuss at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the people had come earlier. I came just before 2.00 p.m. Most of the people were already in town and they had been discussing their impressions of what they saw. Everything looked so terrible that, quite simply, people felt terrible about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you say anything at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the officer did most of the speaking. I think he sort of held a lecture, he lectured us. I did not expect to come to a meeting and be lectured. It was said that there was military rule in the town and that there was no civilian parent authority and that the government had nothing to look for there, that nothing could be done without the army, and on that occasion or -- I asked, "What are we going to do when you leave? How are we going to supply the population with food?" I asked whether it would be the army who was going to do the harvesting because there were still some crops that could be saved, and what were we going to eat the following year? I think that I only took the floor once and for a very brief moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What else was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite recall. But generally speaking, I was disappointed and I think the other people were disappointed in the manner in which they were received.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was any discussion of prisoners of war, officers or civilians? Do you remember whether anything was discussed of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. Perhaps -- there was a lot of talk there in circles. It was not a regular meeting. It is possible that some groups discussed prisoners of war. I myself did not know that prisoners of war existed. But what was discussed was what to do with the people there. I think the officer's name was Vojnovic, and I think he said that that is up to the army and that we have nothing to do there, with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, as you say, the meeting lasted about one hour. After the meeting, you left the room and you went into the yard of VELEPROMET. Is there any one entrance and exit from that particular room when you had the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Afterwards, was anybody waiting for you outside?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was at the meeting and Leskovac was with us. I'm not sure that he attended the meeting the whole time. He walked about a lot. The people who were waiting were those people from Kladovo and Jagodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, we discussed how you left Backa Palanka, who was with you, and so on and so forth. Could you tell us who left and how you left Backa Palanka, how you came to VELEPROMET, whether you used the same road to go there and to get back?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we left Backa Palanka, I think that it was somewhere after noon, after 12.00. Three cars, one car was driven by Leskovac; in another car, a red Lada Niva, that was the make of the vehicle, was Cvetkovic and Lazarevic, Nebojsa, Jevtovic and myself; and in the third car, there was Tomasevic and Mirko, the professor, and the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened to Leskovac's car?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Leskovac drove his car so that we could go back to Banovci because Cvetkovic was stationed there and the two of us had to return to Trpinja where we lived, but there was a puncture in the car tyre so he -- the car stayed there and we moved to the other car, the Niva, which was a terrain vehicle. The road was bad. There was a lot of mud on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that is how you entered VELEPROMET. At the end of the meeting, did they wait for you, for the meeting to finish?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you leave VELEPROMET in that same composition, using two cars, two vehicles now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you go from the VELEPROMET compound?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We went towards the town, down into town, we passed the Orthodox church and the administrative building of VELEPROMET on the right-hand side, we passed the children's first aid shed and we turned left, which was where the army was stationed, and we could not pass through that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we see the tape again from the moment of departure from the VELEPROMET compound?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that how you left the compound?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you hear your voice, your own voice, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's Leskovac and I. That's me. That is me talking. Once again, my voice. That's my voice again. That's me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where are you moving towards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We're moving towards the centre of town, that is towards the Orthodox church and towards the children's clinic. That's my voice again. That is the administrative building. That is the cross-roads with the Ivoandric Street and the children's clinic and the old building of the SDK. We stopped here because we couldn't go any further, at least we couldn't go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you leave the town, please tell us. When you leave the centre of town, please tell us. Is that your voice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is my interview, my interview to a reporter of radio calling -- Tomasevic is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that still your voice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You're giving your interview to Radio Polinje (phoen).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that the same road you took?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same road as we took towards VELEPROMET. According to the information that we had, it was the only road that could be traversed, the only open road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are now moving where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We're moving -- we're going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We are going up the street that we went down a moment ago. That's my voice again. That's also my voice. That's my voice again. We're leaving Vukovar. These are the last houses in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you're on the road to Negoslavci from whence we came. May we take the tape back a little to 1543 -- 1542? May we take the tape back to 1442, please, the technicians? Rewind the tape to 1442. So you're leaving Vukovar and are on the road to Negoslavci. There are some buses there. Did you stop there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we caught up with a column of people who were being taken from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Between that place and Vukovar, you went along the straight road or did you turn off anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's the straight road to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you turn off the road at any point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For a time you worked in Vupik and in Ovcara in the course of your lifetime. You know where the road leads off to Ovcara. Is that turnoff before or after that house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there's no house there. There are no houses at the road that turns off.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 58. It is the map of Vukovar which was shown to Witness D or B. Would you please put this on the ELMO so that you could show it then?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please show us on this map where Vukovar is and where you went and where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the road from Negoslavci to Vukovar. We were going back and on our way there --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm talking about your way back, on your way out of Vukovar. We're going back this way.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: From Vukovar we went straight to Negoslavci, Orolik and further on -- yes, Negoslavci, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where is the turnoff to Ovcara on this road?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Somebody marked it. Probably somebody used this map. Over here approximately, where it should be. I cannot say with certainty whether it is here or 500 metres left or right but approximately there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it halfway between Vukovar and Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So approximately that's it. So you had to pass that in order to get to the last photograph or, rather, the last shot on the tape; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We came -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But no dilemma about this turning off.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before I ask you, why did you go -- why did you go back the same way because there is a road which is closer?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we had, the only road that was open and that the army allowed traffic on was that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But in Sidski Banovci there was a car waiting; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were many reasons, because of the delegation that came from Kladovo who wanted to see Vukovar and we had to pass that way. But at any rate, according to the information that we had, that was the only way -- the only road that the army allowed for traffic. I don't know if somebody else could have passed some other way, but we couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After you stayed there in Negoslavci -- I mean, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say exactly. In Negoslavci, we didn't have any major problems. We stopped once, and we also tried to overtake some buses when we were stopped by a big group of soldiers. They stood in front of us and they cursed at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you continued?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After a few minutes, you went on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you stop then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We stopped next at the entrance to the village of Orolik, we were there in a column of buses and some other vehicles that were transporting the population of Vukovar. We got out of that column and we started moving towards the barrier. It wasn't a classical barrier, it was an improvised barrier made of an Acacia branch and it was down. A soldier stood there and he didn't let us pass through. I was sitting in front next to Mr. Cvetkovic who was driving the car, and I got out and I asked him to let us pass, and I showed him the pass I had, but he very rudely answered me, insulting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tell us what he said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't. It's not decent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But could you sort of try to describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said, "Who fucks you in your government? I'm the government here." And I responded to that, and I said, "How can you behave that way, you young whipper-snapper?" This was a very young man. "You don't even know who I am and you are so rude." And at that point, the others got out of the vehicle, and there were other people there from cars that were behind us, there were quite a few civilian cars there, so some other people got out and watched this. And, at one point, some other soldiers came here, two, five, I don't know how many, I can't remember exactly, and at one point -- from a house that was from the other side. We were facing Orolik. An officer walked out and Mr. Cvetkovic also got out of the car, and he was wearing a uniform, and I think the situation then calmed down. I think it lasted some 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did somebody draw their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This first young man who stopped us. I remembered him. I shall remember him all my life. He had a dark complexion. I don't want anyone to feel offended by this, so I hope no one will mind, but he is of Romany descent, he was rather short, and he pointed a rifle at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What time could have this been?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was dusk, I imagine it was sometime before 5.00 p.m., before 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then we went to Sidski Banovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Sidski Banovci?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the road was in bad shape. It's not very far away, but the road was muddy so one had to drive slowly because of the holes made by the tanks and others. So I think we arrived sometime before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Sidski Banovci and then how did you move further on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then we parted. Tomasevic and Zoran Jevtovic left earlier, and Nebojsa Lazarevic left together with us in this other car, Leskovac and I in his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what is "his" car?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Leskovac's car. And then we went again via Sid, Backa Palanka, Odzaci, Bac -- Bac, Odzaci, I mean, Bogojevo, Erdut, and we came back. Leskovac brought me some -- to Trpinja sometime before 8.00 and he stayed for a certain period of time at my place, I don't know how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you were going there from the centre of town until you arrived in Sid, was it the same composition of people who were there? I mean, in the car, up to Sidski Banovci, I mean, in the Lada Niva?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The same people who left VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was in front? The Lada Niva?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Lada Niva. Jova Cvetkovic was driving, I was sitting next to him, and in the back seat were Jevtovic, Lazarevic, and Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in the other car?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the other car was the driver Ivezic, Tomasevic, and this professor, Mirko.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During this period of time, until you arrived in Sidski Banovci, during this entire day of the 20th, or even after that, were you at the place of Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not. I was not there. That is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: ... in the indictment. If it were nonsense, you wouldn't be sitting here. Throughout this period, did you know that there was an evacuation of the hospital that was underway and that some people were taken from the hospital in buses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That they stopped somewhere at the army barracks, the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How far away is the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: From VELEPROMET, when you go from -- to the town perhaps, 500 metres on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know during the day that they had passed at all?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, as you talked to the investigators of the Tribunal, had they told you to come to The Hague, would you have come?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I told the gentleman who came to see me, Mr. Curtis. I said that I was prepared to make a statement and, if necessary, to come to The Hague. But I -- I -- I didn't even think about the possibility that I would find myself in this situation, in this humiliating situation. I was prepared to come here and to clarify matters. What was done to me was extremely humiliating, and never in my life have I been more humiliated than when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you were going then to this alleged meeting with Mr. Klein in Vukovar, were you afraid of The Hague Tribunal or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I trusted the Tribunal. I had the guarantees of Mr. Curtis, and I trusted him and I trusted Mr. Klein because he came in accordance with the agreement that I signed. I was one of the signatories. I did not have any right not to trust him. But I didn't trust the Croatian police because they could have arrested me because of the indictment that they had issued against me because of armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the question of the Defence attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you ask your question again, please? The interpreters didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I forgot it, Your Honour. I'll take a look now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question was: Would you have reported to The Hague Tribunal had Mr. Curtis offered us the possibility to come here rather than to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would have come in. I have nothing to be ashamed of, nor am I to be blamed for anything, nor am I guilty of anything. I did not commit any crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You would have at least had the advantage of having voluntarily surrendered yourself. One of the parts is not in the transcript. How did you move towards Sidski Banovci? Who went in Lada Niva and who went in the other car?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Lada Niva, Mr. Cvetkovic was driving and I was sitting next to him on the right-hand side. In the back seat were Leskovac, Lazarevic, and Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And near Sidski Banovci, who left and with whom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: From Sidski Banovci. You mean on the way back?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From Sidski Banovci, what happens after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Jova Cvetkovic stayed in Sidski Banovci; Lazarevic, with his driver, left in his car; and Leskovac and I took his car. We went back to Trpinja. He brought me to Trpinja and then he went to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And just one more detail and that concludes my questioning. During that day, the 20th, did you hear something about Zlatko Vodicka and his wife?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (redacted). Who was Zlatko Vodicka? Please calm down, Mr. Dokmanovic. I will be over in five minutes and then you will rest until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you want us to adjourn until tomorrow, maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, this is the last question I have, if he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic can calm down. Probably it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.11 p.m. to be reconvened Thursday, 28 May, 1998, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
